title: Inside Day
teaches: The inside day as we trade it: a quiet bar whose high and low both sit inside the prior day's, used as an entry tool inside a bigger setup in a leader above its 200-day, bought as price trades over the high, with the stop a few cents under the inside day's low, the buy off if the low trades first, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and the knowledge that the bar alone is near random while the stock, the location and the market carry the edge.

walkthroughs.title: NVDA, January 2024: TraderLion's own example
steps: NVDA, 2024. A breakout, then four days later an inside day on light volume, above a rising 50 and 200-day.
The bar is small, 36% of the mother bar, and quiet. Location first: days after a breakout in a leader.
2024-01-16: it opens 0.1% over the trigger. Buy the open at market, 55.02. Stop a few cents under the inside low, 54.28.
Failure mode: the break lasts a day and the stop goes. Instead 3R comes in two days. First sell is judgment.

walkthroughs.title: MPC, January 2013: at the 10-day after a shelf
steps: MPC, 2013. A two-week shelf at the 10-day, then an inside day closing near its high on 0.66x the mother bar's volume.
Quiet, light, at the 10-day: the location carries the trade, not the bar.
2013-01-15: price trades over the high. Buy at market, 31.33. Stop a few cents under the low, 30.90, 1.37% away.
Failure mode: the low trades first, or the break lasts a day. Instead 3R came the next day. No day-one sell.

walkthroughs.title: VST, December 2023: the slow one and the trail
steps: VST, 2023. A plain inside day at the 10-day in a slow, orderly trend. Nothing dramatic about the bar.
2023-12-22: price trades over the high. Buy at market, 38.00. Stop a few cents under the inside day's low, 37.53.
Failure mode: a stall still under 1R after 10 days is sold. Instead it reaches 3R on day 10.
First sell by judgment, then trail the rest. In our test, buys without a trail lose on average.

questions.q: What makes today an inside day?
choices: Both ends inside yesterday's range
A close well inside yesterday's range
The narrowest range in seven days
An open inside yesterday's range
questions.answer: Both ends inside yesterday's range
questions.why: Both ends inside yesterday's range: today's high is below yesterday's high and today's low is above yesterday's low. Crabel, Bulkowski, Mish and TraderLion all describe the whole day fitting inside the prior day. The close and the open do not decide it. A narrow day, such as an NR7, can still poke out.
questions.lesson_line: Both ends inside yesterday's bar. That is the whole definition.

wrong.A close well inside yesterday's range: The close is not the test. The high and the low are, and both must be inside.
wrong.The narrowest range in seven days: That is an NR7, the narrowest range in seven days. A narrow day can still poke above yesterday's high.
wrong.An open inside yesterday's range: The open is only one price. The high and the low of the whole day must sit inside.

questions.simple: An inside day has a high and a low that both sit inside yesterday's high and low.

reasons: five sources agree; the key uses only the part that strict and tie rules share

questions.story: The last bar on the chart is today.

questions.q: The inside day is a setup by itself.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The inside day is an entry tool inside a bigger setup, not a setup by itself. The bar alone is near random. The stock, the location and the market carry the edge.
questions.lesson_line: The inside day is how you get in. The setup is what you are getting into.
questions.simple: False. The inside day is only a way to get in, and the stock, the location and the market carry the edge.

reasons: one source: the criteria card, a proposed criterion

questions.q: Where does the stop go on an inside-day buy?
choices: A few cents under the inside low
A few cents under the mother low
A few cents under the entry price
Seven percent under the fill price
questions.answer: A few cents under the inside low
questions.why: A few cents under the inside day's low, not exactly on it. Never use the mother bar's low just to give it room. The stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. If the stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Kullamagi also puts the stop at the low of the day. Bulkowski's 7% loss limit is not our rule.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the inside day's low.

wrong.A few cents under the mother low: That is the named mistake: the mother low to give it room, then sizing as if it were tight.
wrong.Seven percent under the fill price: That is Bulkowski's loss limit, not ours. Our stop is the inside day's low, usually within about 3%.
wrong.A few cents under the entry price: That is not the inside day's low. The stop sits under the low; breakeven comes later in the trade.

questions.simple: Put the stop a few cents under the inside day's low, never the mother bar's low just for room.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)
fixed before

questions.story: The inside day, the day before the buy.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: An inside-day buy needs the close above the ___-day, with the 50-day above it.
questions.why: 200. The inside-day card needs the close above the 200-day, with the 50-day above the 200-day. That keeps us out of longs below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200, the 50 over the 200. Then look at the bar.
questions.simple: It is the 200-day, because we buy no longs below that line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: The mother bar is the day the inside day sits inside.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The mother bar is our name for the day the inside day sits inside. The whole inside day falls within it: its high is lower and its low is higher.
questions.lesson_line: Two bars: the mother bar, and the quiet day inside it.
questions.simple: True. The mother bar is the bigger day that holds the inside day within its range.

reasons: a naming convention from the card, not a word the web sources use

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A double inside day is ___ inside days in a row, each inside the day before.
questions.answer: two
questions.why: Two. A double inside day is two inside days in a row, each inside the day before. A triple is three. Mish says two in a row is an even clearer sign of indecision.
questions.lesson_line: Two quiet days, each inside the last. The spring winds tighter.
questions.simple: Two. A double inside day is two quiet days in a row, each one inside the day before.

reasons: the card's alternate reading of a double also gives two

questions.q: Volume lighter than the mother bar is preferred on an inside day, not required.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Lighter than the mother bar is preferred, not required. TraderLion: best when the inside bar comes on low volume; Morpheus wants it on lighter volume too.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet volume on the quiet day is a plus, not a must.

questions.q: Our research says inside-day buys with a fixed stop and no trims are a loser on average unless something is added. What?
choices: A trail on the winning trades
A wider stop on every buy
A tighter, smaller inside day
A bigger share size on each buy
questions.answer: A trail on the winning trades
questions.why: A trail on the winners. Our research says a fixed stop with no trims is a loser on average unless the winners are trailed. Also, 88.2% were stopped within 60 days. We choose the first sell by judgment, rarely on day 1, and trail the rest. That is our answer to the problem, not a tested result.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength and trail the rest. A fixed stop alone loses on average.

wrong.A wider stop on every buy: A wider stop means fewer shares for the same risk. It does not manage the winners.
wrong.A tighter, smaller inside day: Tinier is not better. A sliver with its low in the noise is the B- end.
wrong.A bigger share size on each buy: A bigger size scales every loss too. The size comes from the stop and the risk percent, not from a wish.

questions.simple: Our research says a fixed stop with no trims loses on average, so the winners need a trail.

deeper.trap: Do not read this as proof that trims and a trail win. The scan used a fixed stop with no trims, so it never tested them. It shows only that the bar needs its winners trailed, and that the bar alone is near random. The trail is the part we add.

reasons: a number from our own test that can be rerun (88.2%)
fixed before

questions.q: The inside day's high is 50.00. What is the highest open we would still buy?
questions.why: 52.00. The open can be at most 4% over the inside day's high: 50.00 x 1.04, which is 52.00.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the high is the line. Work it out before the open.
questions.simple: We buy an open at most 4% over the high, so 50.00 plus 4% is 52.00.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
fixed before

wrong.$48.00: Took 4% off the high. The limit sits above the high.
wrong.$50.20: Slipped the decimal point in the 4%.

questions.q: A clean inside day two sessions before an earnings report is still a buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. Two sessions before is inside that window. We hold through a report only when the trade is already up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Stay three days clear of the report, or wait. A report is a gap you cannot stop.
questions.simple: A buy two sessions before earnings breaks our rule of no new buys in the 3 days before a report.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: What happens to the buy?
choices: It is off; the low traded first
Nothing; keep waiting for the high
Buy now; it is a cheaper price
Not yet; only a close under counts
questions.answer: It is off; the low traded first
questions.why: It is off. If the inside day's low trades first, before the entry, the buy over the high is cancelled. That is the failure mode on our card. A cheaper price is not a reason to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Which side trades first decides the trade. The low first, and the break is off.

wrong.Nothing; keep waiting for the high: The card says the buy over the high is off once the low trades first. Waiting for the high is the old plan.
wrong.Buy now; it is a cheaper price: That price is under the inside day's low, where our stop belongs. A buy there is not this setup.
wrong.Not yet; only a close under counts: The card says the buy over the high is off once the low trades first. It does not wait for a close.

questions.story: Your buy order sits a cent over the inside day's high. The stock opens flat and trades under the inside day's low at 9:45.
questions.simple: The buy is off. The stock broke the inside day's low before it broke the high.

reasons: one source: the criteria card, a proposed criterion

questions.q: We take inside days in leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet bar in a laggard is still a laggard. Buy the leaders.

questions.q: A very narrow inside day, with the stop only 0.8% away. How does it compare with a normal-sized pause?
choices: Not better; narrow is not a plus
Better; tighter is stronger
Better; its stop is smaller
The same; only shape counts
questions.answer: Not better; narrow is not a plus
questions.why: Not better. Do not treat a tiny inside day, an NR4 or an NR7 as better. A sliver's low sits inside the day's noise, so it is the weak end.
questions.lesson_line: A sliver is not a tight stop. Its low sits in the noise.

wrong.Better; tighter is stronger: The card says not to treat a tiny inside day, an NR4 or an NR7 as better.
wrong.Better; its stop is smaller: The stop only sets the share count. Our risk is the percent we set, and a stop that small sits inside the day's noise.
wrong.The same; only shape counts: Size counts. A tiny sliver is not better, and its low sits in the noise.

questions.simple: Not better. A very narrow day is not a plus, because its low sits in the noise.

deeper.counter: An NR7 is the narrowest range in seven days, and an NR4 the narrowest in four. That says a day is quiet, not that it is better. Our card does not treat a tiny inside day, an NR4 or an NR7 as better.

reasons: one source for the key: the criteria card, a cue
fixed before

questions.q: Buy the break?
choices: No; Red is mostly cash and shorts
Yes; a leader is a leader, so buy
Yes, but at half the usual size
Short it; Red favors shorts
questions.answer: No; Red is mostly cash and shorts
questions.why: No. In a Red reading we are mostly in cash and shorts. Green or Yellow is when we take this setup, and Orange is A+ only. The reading is a guide, but the stock and the bar can be perfect and the market still says no.
questions.lesson_line: The best bar in a Red market is a bar. Sit on your hands.

wrong.Yes; a leader is a leader, so buy: The stock is one of three things that carry the edge. The market is another, and it says no.
wrong.Yes, but at half the usual size: Half size does not change the reading. Red is mostly cash and shorts.
wrong.Short it; Red favors shorts: Our shorts sit below the 200-day, and this leader is above it. Red cuts buying; it does not turn a leader into a short.

questions.story: The reading is Red. A leader above its 200-day prints a clean inside day after a breakout.
questions.simple: No, because a Red market means mostly cash and shorts, even for a good leader.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)
fixed before

questions.q: How do we buy the break over this inside day's high?
choices: At market as it trades over the high
A limit order under the low
A limit order a cent over the high
In premarket on a gap up
questions.answer: At market as it trades over the high
questions.why: At market, once it trades over the high, in regular hours. Entries are market orders, bought as price trades through the high. There are no new buys outside regular trading hours, so a premarket gap is not bought there. A limit under the low waits for the very weakness that cancels the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Market order, regular hours, as it trades through. No limit, no premarket.

wrong.A limit order under the low: A limit under the low waits for the very weakness that cancels the buy.
wrong.In premarket on a gap up: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
wrong.A limit order a cent over the high: Entries are market orders, not limit orders.

questions.simple: We buy at market as price trades over the high, and only in regular hours.

deeper.trap: The trap is the careful-looking limit order. A limit under the low waits for the weakness that cancels the buy. Our entries are market orders, bought as price trades over the high.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58) and a held decision on entry timing
fixed before

questions.story: The inside day, the day before the break.

questions.q: Bought at 20.71 with the stop at 20.47. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 21.43. One R is the fill minus the stop: 20.71 minus 20.47. Add three of those to the fill, 20.71. We use 3R as a measuring stick, not a sell order. JBLU got there the next day.
questions.lesson_line: A small stop makes 3R a small move. Know the number before the open.
questions.simple: Three R is the fill plus three times the distance down to the stop, so 21.43.

reasons: a computed key

wrong.$21.19: Added three R to the stop instead of to the fill.
wrong.$19.99: Subtracted three R. A long's target sits above the fill.
wrong.$23.71: Added 3 dollars, not three R. R is the fill minus the stop.

questions.story: Bought on the break the day after the inside day.

questions.q: An inside day in a pullback, closing under its 20 EMA. Our read?
choices: A pause in a range, not a setup
A buy; any inside day will work
Skip it; the bar is too narrow
A continuation; buy over its high
questions.answer: A pause in a range, not a setup
questions.why: Not this setup. A close under the 20 EMA before the entry invalidates it. An inside day under the fast average is a pause in a range, not a continuation.
questions.lesson_line: Under the fast average, a quiet day is a stall, not a spring.

wrong.A buy; any inside day will work: Buying every inside day is the named mistake. The location decides.
wrong.A continuation; buy over its high: An inside day under the fast average is a pause in a range, not a continuation.
wrong.Skip it; the bar is too narrow: A narrow bar is not banned. The reason to skip is the close under the 20 EMA.

questions.simple: Skip it. After a close under the 20 EMA, a quiet day is only a pause in a range.

reasons: one source: the criteria card, a proposed criterion
fixed before

questions.story: The last bar on the chart is the inside day.

questions.q: The full fast stack of the 8, 21 and 50-day is required before an inside-day buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The full stack of the 8, 21 and 50-day is a cue, not a requirement. One hard test is a close above the 200-day, with the 50-day above it. Our rule is no longs below the 200-day, except a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: The stack is a plus. A close above the 200-day is the test.
questions.simple: False. The stack is only a cue, and one hard test is a close above the 200-day, with the 50-day over it.

reasons: rests on the hard 200-day rule in the rulebook

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: An inside-day trade still under 1R after ___ trading days is sold.
questions.why: 10. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, which frees the money for a better setup. 1R is what you risk on the trade, the gap from your entry to your stop. StockCharts says a short-term setup should start working right away, but it does not set our 10 days.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: We sell a trade that is still under 1R after 10 trading days, to free the money.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: A clean inside day at the 20-day with an unfilled bearish gap 2% above. What does the gap do to the grade?
choices: Lowers it; no clear air above
Nothing; only the bar is graded
Raises it; the gap is a target
Rules it out; the trade is void
questions.answer: Lowers it; no clear air above
questions.why: Lowers it. Room means clear air to the next level. A bearish gap or an old high just overhead is the B- end. That is a lower grade, not a ban on the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Check the room above before you buy. A gap or old high just overhead lowers the grade.

wrong.Nothing; only the bar is graded: Room is graded too. A bearish gap just overhead is the B- end.
wrong.Raises it; the gap is a target: Room means clear air to the next level. A bearish gap overhead is the B- end, not a plus.
wrong.Rules it out; the trade is void: Room is a grade cue. A bearish gap just overhead is the B- end, a lower grade, not a ban.

questions.simple: The gap lowers the grade, because a bearish gap just overhead leaves no clear air to run.

reasons: one cited fact only (a proposed grade cue)

questions.q: Bulkowski expects an inside day to break out in the direction of the trend going in.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Bulkowski says to expect the breakout in the same direction as the inbound trend. TraderLion also says price hints at continuing in its current direction. It is an expectation, not a guarantee. Bulkowski does not require a trend, so we add the 200-day gate ourselves.
questions.lesson_line: A pause can resume the trend. So we want a leader in an uptrend.
questions.simple: True. Bulkowski expects the breakout to follow the trend going in, but it is only an expectation.

reasons: a pattern expectation from the web, not a guarantee

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Pass; wait for a tighter trigger
Use the mother low; size down
Pull the stop to 3%; size down
Keep the stop; buy the usual size
questions.answer: Pass; wait for a tighter trigger
questions.why: Pass and wait for a tighter trigger. We prefer 1 to 3%, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% is acceptable. This stop is 6% from the trigger, so we mostly wait. The stop stays under the inside day's low. Never use the mother low to give it room.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

wrong.Use the mother low; size down: Never use the mother low just to give it room. The stop stays under the inside day's low.
wrong.Pull the stop to 3%; size down: A 3% stop sits above the inside day's low. Never move the stop up to make a trade fit.
wrong.Keep the stop; buy the usual size: The same shares on a wider stop risk more than planned. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

questions.story: The inside day is wide: the stop under its low sits 6% from the trigger. The mother bar's low is 8% away.
questions.simple: Pass and wait for a tighter trigger, because this stop is past the 5% we accept.

deeper.counter: A wide stop is not a flaw in the setup. It is information. Up to 5% is acceptable, with the size set by the stop. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger, never the same shares with the stop moved closer.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5) and a stop-size line still held

questions.q: Bought at 41.09 with the stop at 40.45. How far below the buy is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 1.56%. The gap is the buy minus the stop: 41.09 minus 40.45. Divide by the buy, 41.09, and show it as a percent. That is well inside the 3% habit for the stop. ATI's inside day gave a small stop.
questions.lesson_line: Trigger minus stop, over the trigger. Inside days give small stops.
questions.simple: Take the buy minus the stop, divide by the buy, and you get 1.56%.

reasons: a computed key

wrong.0.64%: Read the dollar gap as a percent. Divide it by the buy first.
wrong.15.58%: Slipped the decimal point one place right.
wrong.98.44%: Divided the stop by the buy. That is how much of the price is left, not how far the stop is.

questions.story: Bought on the break the day after the inside day.

questions.q: The inside day ran 20.00 to 21.00 and closed at 20.80. Where in its range did it close, 0 to 1?
questions.why: 0.8, near the high. Close minus low: 20.80 minus 20.00. Divide by high minus low: 21.00 minus 20.00. A close in the upper half of the inside day's range is preferred. It is a grading cue, not a rule.
questions.lesson_line: Close minus low, over high minus low. Near the top is the picture we like.
questions.simple: The close is 0.8 of the way up the day's range, so it sits near the high.

reasons: a computed key
cue or rule is a held decision
fixed before

wrong.0.99: Divided the close by the high. Use the range: close minus low, over high minus low.
wrong.1.04: Divided the close by the low instead of by the range.
wrong.1.25: Flipped it: range over climb instead of climb over range.

questions.q: What now?
choices: Out now; the loss is past 2R
New stop is the 46.70 low
Hold for the gap to fill
Sell half, hold the rest
questions.answer: Out now; the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Out. A gap through the stop hands it to the first 30-minute low, with a ceiling: past 2R, get out. One R is the buy minus the stop. The low of 46.70 is further below the buy than two of those.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception, and it has a ceiling of 2R.

wrong.New stop is the 46.70 low: The 30-minute low becomes the stop only while the loss is inside 2R. This one is past it, so you are out.
wrong.Hold for the gap to fill: Hope is not a rule. The gap rule has a ceiling, and this is past it.
wrong.Sell half, hold the rest: Past 2R the rule is get out, not scale out. Half now and half hoped for is not the plan.

questions.story: You bought the break at 50.00 with the stop at 48.70. The next morning it gaps open at 47.80. The first 30-minute bar's low is 46.70.
questions.simple: The first 30-minute low is more than 2R below the buy, so the rule says get out.

deeper.counter: The gap open was already below the stop, so a stop order alone could not protect you. The first 30 minutes then decide. Inside 2R the first 30-minute low is the new stop. Past 2R you are out. This is the one place the stop is allowed to move down, and it has a ceiling.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
the key is a computed comparison in R

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
choices: Sell a third at the open
Wait for the close to sell
Sell it all at the open
Just raise the stop; no trim
questions.answer: Sell a third at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, we take that trim at the open. This one opens at 3.5R, past the 3R level, so the first third comes off. The rest stays in with its stop.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through a trim level is the trim. Take it at the open.

wrong.Wait for the close to sell: We take the trim at the open, not later. A stock that opens above a trim level gets that trim at the open.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: The trim is a third at 3R. The rest stays in with its stop.
wrong.Just raise the stop; no trim: Raising the stop is a separate step. A trim level the open has passed is taken at the open.

questions.story: Your inside-day long sits at 2.7R at the close. It opens the next morning at 3.5R.
questions.simple: The open is already past 3R, so we sell the first third right at the open.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)

questions.q: Mish's 2009 AAPL inside-day buy sat about 17% under its long-term average. What decides whether we take it?
choices: The 200-day rule; it fails it
The pattern; it was textbook
The market; it was a bottom
The size; we would go half
questions.answer: The 200-day rule; it fails it
questions.why: The 200-day rule. The inside-day card needs the close above the 200-day, and Mish's AAPL buy sat about 17% under it. So it fails our rule, however well the example worked.
questions.lesson_line: Other people's rules can be right for them. The 200-day line is ours.

wrong.The pattern; it was textbook: The pattern is an entry tool. The card needs the close above the 200-day first.
wrong.The market; it was a bottom: Bottoms are known later. The rule is known before: the card needs the close above the 200-day.
wrong.The size; we would go half: Size does not lift the 200-day line. The inside-day card needs the close above it.

questions.simple: The 200-day rule decides it, because that buy sat about 17% under the line and the card needs the close above it.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski finds no trend is required into an inside day; the trend is upward 53% of the time. Our card asks for more, the close above the 200-day. A good example on the wrong side of the line is still a pass.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: Yesterday ran 52.00 to 49.00. Which day today is an inside day?
questions.why: High 51.50, low 49.50. Both ends sit inside yesterday's range of 49.00 to 52.00: the high is under 52.00 and the low is over 49.00. One end inside is not enough.
questions.lesson_line: Check both ends. One end inside is half a definition.

wrong.High 51.00, low 48.50: The high is inside, but the low is under 49.00. Both ends must be inside.
wrong.High 53.00, low 48.00: Both ends poke out. That day covers yesterday's whole range.
wrong.High 52.40, low 51.00: The low is inside, but the high is above 52.00. Both ends must be inside.

questions.simple: Only that day has a high under 52.00 and a low over 49.00, so both ends sit inside.

reasons: a plain comparison of the question's own numbers; three sources agree

questions.q: On an inside-day trade the stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. Where the first sell lands is a judgment call, not a fixed 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R. The first sell is a judgment call.
questions.simple: True, because we move the stop to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)
fixed before

questions.q: Which trade is it now?
choices: The reclaim, with its own stop
Buy over the high, as planned
No trade; the low broke first

questions.q: Write the plan.
choices: Buy 55.02, stop 54.28, first sell day 3+
Buy 55.02, stop 52.00, and hold it all
Wait for the close; mother-low stop
Buy 55.02, stop 54.28, sell half day 1
questions.answer: Buy 55.02, stop 54.28, first sell day 3+
questions.why: Buy the open at market, 55.02. Stop a few cents under the inside low, 54.28. The first sell is a judgment call. We very rarely sell on day 1 and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Then the rest trails.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell, trail. Write it before the open; execute it without a debate.

wrong.Buy 55.02, stop 52.00, and hold it all: The stop belongs a few cents under the inside day's low, 54.28. And the plan needs a first sell and a trail.
wrong.Wait for the close; mother-low stop: We buy as price trades through the high, never at the close. The mother low is the named mistake.
wrong.Buy 55.02, stop 54.28, sell half day 1: The stop is right, but we very rarely sell on day 1. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.

questions.story: An inside day four days after a breakout, on light volume. The next session opens a hair over the high.
questions.simple: Buy at market, put the stop just under the inside low, and wait until day 3 to make the first sell.

deeper.example: Walk the plan in R. The inside low sets one R at 55.02 minus 54.28. R is the measuring stick, not the sell signal. The first sell waits for day 3 at the earliest, then the rest trails the 9 EMA or the 20 EMA. Written before the open, the plan leaves nothing to argue about when the stock moves.

reasons: entry timing is a held decision (D-003)

questions.q: What does Yellow change?
choices: Smaller and fewer than in Green
Nothing; Yellow acts like Green
Only A+ setups get taken
Mostly cash, plus shorts only
questions.answer: Smaller and fewer than in Green
questions.why: Smaller and fewer. The market reading is a guide. Green is full risk per grade and up to 10 positions. Yellow is smaller and fewer. Orange takes only A+ setups, and Red is mostly cash and shorts. Inside days are for Green or Yellow.
questions.lesson_line: Yellow is still a go, but smaller and fewer.

wrong.Nothing; Yellow acts like Green: Green is full risk and up to 10 positions. Yellow is smaller and fewer.
wrong.Only A+ setups get taken: A+ only is Orange. Yellow is smaller and fewer, and the card takes inside days in Green or Yellow.
wrong.Mostly cash, plus shorts only: That is Red. In Yellow the inside days on your list can still be taken, smaller and fewer.

questions.story: The reading is Yellow. Two inside days sit on your list.
questions.simple: Yellow means you still trade, but smaller and fewer than in Green.

deeper.trap: The reading is a guide. Yellow means smaller and fewer than Green. The setup must still pass every other rule.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's market reading, a guide that may change

questions.q: Buy again?
choices: Yes; a new trade, its own stop
No; one try per stock each week
Yes, with the stop under Monday's low
Yes, at double size to win it back
questions.answer: Yes; a new trade, its own stop
questions.why: Yes. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Here a new inside day printed and its high traded. The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. This is the second try this week.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict on the setup. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.Yes, with the stop under Monday's low: The stop is under the new inside day's low. Monday's low belongs to the old trade.
wrong.No; one try per stock each week: The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock, not one.
wrong.Yes, at double size to win it back: A new trade follows every rule, sizing included. The size comes from the stop and the risk percent, not from the last loss.

questions.story: You bought an inside-day break on Monday, your first try on this stock this week, and were stopped out. Wednesday prints a new inside day and Thursday trades over its high.
questions.simple: Yes. A stop-out does not end the stock, and a fresh trigger is a new trade with its own stop and every rule.

deeper.trap: The pull after a loss is to size up and win it back. A re-entry is a new trade with every rule. The tries still count toward 3 a week and 6 a month.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's re-entry and tries rules

questions.q: What do you watch for?
choices: An inside day or two after it
Buy at once, even 6% over the buy point
A deep pullback to the 200-day
A narrow-range day, an NR7
questions.answer: An inside day or two after it
questions.why: An inside day or two after it. The breakout is the setup, and the inside day is the entry tool inside it. UCT's Sunday Scan on SHOP says the same: if you are not in, look for an inside day or two.
questions.lesson_line: Missed the breakout, so watch for the quiet day after it. That is the second door.

wrong.A deep pullback to the 200-day: The note says an inside day or two right after the breakout, not a deep pullback.
wrong.A narrow-range day, an NR7: A narrow-range day can still poke above the prior high. The note asks for an inside day or two.
wrong.Buy at once, even 6% over the buy point: We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Waiting for the quiet day gives a level and a stop.

questions.story: A leader breaks out of a base on Friday. You are not in.
questions.simple: Watch for an inside day or two after the breakout. That quiet bar gives you a clear entry and stop.

deeper.example: UCT's Sunday Scan on SHOP said it finally broke out on Friday. If you were not in, look for an inside day or two.

reasons: rests on the owner's published Sunday Scan words

questions.q: Which is the better inside-day buy?
questions.answer: A; more room, better market
questions.why: A. Both are leaders above the 200-day, but A has clear air and a Green market. B has an old high just overhead, the B- end. The indexes are printing inside days, so we wait for the break. The bar is the same; the stock, the spot and the market carry the edge.
questions.lesson_line: Same bar, different spot. The stock, the room and the market decide which one we buy.
questions.story: Two inside days on different days, both leaders above the 200-day. A: just after a breakout, Green market, clear air overhead. B: under an old high just overhead, with the indexes printing inside days.
choices: A; more room, better market
B; the old high is a target
B; the indexes are coiling up
Equal; the bar is the same

wrong.Equal; the bar is the same: The bar is the same, but the room and the market differ. They carry the edge, not the bar alone.
wrong.B; the old high is a target: An old high just overhead is the B- end of the room, not a target.
wrong.B; the indexes are coiling up: Inside days in the indexes mean wait for the break. Contraction comes before expansion, in either direction.

questions.simple: A is the better buy, because its room and its market line up and B's do not.

deeper.trap: The trap is to grade the bar. Both are inside days above the 200-day, so the bar does not separate them. Look at the room overhead and the market behind it. The stop still sits under the inside day's low.

reasons: the A+ and B- location rows are a held decision (D-066)
fixed before

questions.q: An inside day days after a breakout. Is it above the 200-day with the 50-day over it? Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; the lines are stacked
Pass; price is under the 200-day
Pass; the 50-day is under the 200
Take it; the tiny bar is better
questions.answer: Take it; the lines are stacked
questions.why: Take it. The inside day sits above a rising 50-day and 200-day, with the 50-day over the 200-day. It came four days after a breakout, on light volume. The break came the next session and reached 3R in two days.
questions.lesson_line: Check the lines and the location before the bar. Stacked, after a breakout: that is the spot.

wrong.Pass; the 50-day is under the 200: Look again: the 50-day runs above the 200-day.
wrong.Pass; price is under the 200-day: Price sits above the 200-day on this chart, days after a breakout.
wrong.Take it; the tiny bar is better: A tiny inside day is not better. The reason to take it is the location: above the 200-day, with the 50 over it.

questions.simple: Take it. The price is above the 200-day, the 50-day is over it, and this is days after a breakout.

deeper.trap: Do the lines first, then the bar. An inside day under the 200-day is not ours, however clean it looks. The full stack of the 8, 21 and 50-day is only a cue.

reasons: rests on the hard 200-day rule
the chart read rests on the dossier

questions.q: Is the last bar an inside day? Take the break over its high, or pass.
choices: Pass; its high is above yesterday's
Take it; the narrowest day in a week
Take it; its low is inside yesterday's
Pass; the bar is too narrow to trade
questions.answer: Pass; its high is above yesterday's
questions.why: Pass. The high is 0.30% above the prior day's high, while the low is 1.26% inside. Both ends must be inside. So this is a narrow-range day after a breakout, not an inside day.
questions.lesson_line: Narrow is not inside. The high gives it away.

wrong.Take it; the narrowest day in a week: A narrow day can still poke above yesterday's high. This one did.
wrong.Take it; its low is inside yesterday's: One end inside is half a definition. The high is above yesterday's.
wrong.Pass; the bar is too narrow to trade: A narrow bar is not banned. This one fails because its high is above yesterday's, so it is not an inside day.

questions.simple: Pass. The high is above yesterday's high, so only one end is inside and it is not an inside day.

deeper.trap: Hindsight trap: bought over its high, this bar went 1.7R. That says nothing about the rule. It was a narrow-range day after a breakout, not an inside day. One good result cannot make it one.

reasons: bar numbers read from our own bars
tied to the held decision D-002 on the narrow-range look-alike

questions.q: Your call?
choices: Take it; stock, spot, market agree
Pass; the bar alone is near random
Take it; stop at the mother low
Take it, at half the usual size
questions.answer: Take it; stock, spot, market agree
questions.why: Take it, at market. The bar alone is near random, but the stock, the location and the market carry the edge, and all three agree here. Our Sunday Scans point to this picture: an inside day and a higher low at a rising 20 EMA. The trigger is the trade over the high.
questions.lesson_line: When the stock, the spot and the market all say yes, the quiet day is the door.

wrong.Pass; the bar alone is near random: Alone, yes. Here the stock, the spot and the market all agree, so it is not the bar alone.
wrong.Take it, at half the usual size: The market is Green and the stock, spot and market agree. Green means full risk for the grade. Nothing here calls for half.
wrong.Take it; stop at the mother low: Never use the mother low just to give it room. The stop stays a few cents under the inside day's low.

questions.story: A clean inside day at a rising 20-day in a leader above its 200-day, its 50-day above the 200. Green market, no earnings for weeks, the stop 1.5% under the trigger. The next day at 10:20, the high trades.
questions.simple: Take it, because the stock, the spot and the market all agree, even though the bar alone is near random.

deeper.trap: The trap is to read 'near random' as 'never'. In our test, only 26.7% reached 3R and 88.2% were eventually stopped. The rule set is a filter, not an edge by itself. We buy it where the stock, the spot and the market agree, and manage it with the stop, trims and trail.

reasons: entry timing is a held decision (D-003)

questions.q: A stop kept in your head is enough for an inside-day buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. For an inside-day buy it sits a few cents under the inside day's low.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is not a stop. Use a real order.
questions.simple: False. We use a real stop order with the broker, a few cents under the inside day's low.

deeper.trap: A real stop order is not the whole answer. When a stock gaps open under the stop, our gap rule applies. The first 30-minute low becomes the new stop, and a loss past 2R means out.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's real-stop-order rule

questions.q: Size follows the setup's grade. What happens to the size on a B- setup?
choices: Sized down from normal size
Sized up, as for an A+
Normal size, same as a B
Skipped; A and B only
questions.answer: Sized down from normal size
questions.why: Sized down. Our rule sets size by grade: A and B setups are normal size, A+ is sized up, and B- or lower is sized down. How a setup earns its grade is a judgment call, not a checklist.
questions.lesson_line: Grade sets the size. A+ up, A and B normal, B- down.

wrong.Sized up, as for an A+: A+ setups are sized up. B- or lower is sized down.
wrong.Normal size, same as a B: A and B setups are normal size. B- or lower is sized down.
wrong.Skipped; A and B only: The rule says B- or lower is sized down. It does not say to skip it.

questions.simple: It is sized down. A and B setups are normal size, A+ is sized up, and B- or lower is sized down.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, D38 and E50

questions.q: What do you have after the last close?
questions.story: Judge the last three bars after the last close.
choices: Double inside; the first bar is mother
Triple inside; the first bar counts too
Single inside; only the middle counts
None; the last bar is only narrow
questions.answer: Double inside; the first bar is mother
questions.why: A double inside day. The first of the three bars is the mother bar. The middle bar sits inside it, and the last bar sits inside the middle one. That is two inside days in a row, each inside the day before. Mish says two in a row is an even clearer sign of indecision. It is still an entry tool inside a bigger setup, not a setup by itself.
questions.lesson_line: Count from the mother bar. Each inside day has to sit inside the day before.
questions.simple: A double inside day. The middle bar is inside the first and the last is inside the middle, so that is two in a row.

wrong.Triple inside; the first bar counts too: The first bar is the mother bar, the day the others sit inside. It is not an inside day, so the count is two.
wrong.Single inside; only the middle counts: The last bar sits inside the middle one, so it counts too. A single would stop after the middle bar.
wrong.None; the last bar is only narrow: Both ends of the last bar sit inside the middle bar. A narrow range is no fault, and it is still an inside day.
